newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Finance One faces uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Finance One faces uncertain future.

text.p: The future of Thailand's one-time leading finance company, Finance One Plc, remains uncertain a week after plans for a face-saving merger with Thai Danu Bank Plc fell apart, analysts said on Friday.
Plans to marry the troubled firm off to the medium-sized commercial bank, touted by authorities as a blueprint for consolidation elsewhere in the sector, collapsed last week.
That left Finance One scrambling to formulate a rescue plan which, as it turned out, failed to convince most investors that the company's prospects are particularly bright.
Finance One's shares resumed trading after a three-month suspension on Friday at six baht ($0.24), a 75-percent discount to their last trade on February 28 at 23.75.
Analysts said the discount reflected unease over the company's long-term prospects.
"The interesting question is less where the company will be in 12 or 24 months' time, but will it be?," said Richard Henderson, head of research at broker Krungthai Thanakit Plc.

Pundits said much depends on who buys into Finance One's huge 8.28-billion-baht ($330-million) capital increase, which is due in June. The central bank's Financial Institutions Rehabilitation Fund has pledged to buy all unsubscribed shares.
At a meeting earlier this week, Finance One chairman Pin Chakkapak could not say who -- other than the central bank -- would be buying into the rights issue.
Executives of the firm's two largest shareholders, Thai Farmers Bank Plc and France's Banque Paribas, were unavailable for comment.

Dubbed King Pin by the local media for turning Finance One into Thailand's leading non-bank finance company in the early 1990s, Pin declined to say whether he would personally be buying to prevent dilution of his 3.87 percent stake.
Unless another buyer appears, the Bank of Thailand -- fresh from spending about $2 billion bailing out the Bangkok Bank of Commerce Plc -- will end up as the largest shareholder, analysts said.
"Current shareholders will certainly not want to inject more capital into the firm," predicted Thaimex Finance and Securities Plc in a recent report.

"It is a safe bet...that taxpayers' money (will be put) to work to support and, to a degree, take over FinOne. Once again the taxpayers, most of whom did not participate in the joy ride in the (firm's) heydays, will have to pay for the damage inflicted by unrestrained financial managers," it said.
The capital increase is needed to cover a deteriorating asset base contaminated by now-soured lending to Thailand's troubled real estate market and consumer finance sectors.
At the end of the March this year, 9.5 percent of the firm's 95.5 billion baht of total lending was non-performing.

Though the firm said on Wednesday that the upcoming capital increase is sufficent to ensure financial stability, analysts privately argue that more may be needed to cover a further deterioration in the firm's loan portfolio quality.
Finance One also plans to raise cash by selling stakes in broker Jardine Fleming Thanakom Securities Co Ltd and 49 percent of the securities arm of another subsidiary, Thana One Co Ltd.
Finance One needs cash to pay a coupon on a $120-million Eurobond due in February 1998, to honour domestic debt obligations, repay local lenders and for working capital.
Analysts said Pin's hope of winning a commercial banking licence as part of the rescue appeared a distant possibility.
All this suggests Finance One will emerge from its current problems -- if it emerges at all -- a far smaller and humbler company. ($1 = 25 baht
